matched_finding.subcategory: effect sizes dramatically smaller than original with no discussion
matched_finding.description: The original study reported ηp2 = .06 for the effect of identifiability on donation. The replication reports ηp2 = .007—approximately an eight-fold reduction. Similarly, the original intervention effect was ηp2 = .04; the replication finds ηp2 = .001. While these are random data and thus uninterpretable, the pattern of uniformly tiny effect sizes across all outcomes (most ηp2 ≤ .008) is not discussed in terms of what this would mean for replication evaluation or power. An actual replication showing effects of this magnitude would strongly disconfirm the original study.

ground_truth.modified_snippet: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables;
ground_truth.description: Changed between-subjects to within-subjects — impossible for this intervention (learning about IVE permanently changes cognition); df in ANOVA tables are inconsistent with within-subjects

matched_finding.description: The original studies used a between-subjects design: each participant encountered only one victim type (identifiable or statistical). This replication embeds Studies 1 and 3 into a single within-subjects design. If participants encounter both identifiable and statistical victims, they explicitly compare them, fundamentally altering the psychological mechanism being studied. The identifiable victim effect is precisely about how isolated presentation of a single victim elicits disproportionate affect; within-subjects exposure triggers analytical comparison and demand characteristics, eliminating the very process the study aims to measure. This is a critical methodological deviation that cannot be treated as a 'close replication.'
matched_finding.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables.

matched_finding.description: The procedures section states that 'participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.' This is not random assignment—it is self-selection, which fundamentally destroys the study's ability to make causal inferences. Participants who choose to learn about the identifiable victim effect may systematically differ from those who do not (e.g., in curiosity, prior knowledge, or openness to persuasion). Similarly, those who choose to read about an identifiable victim may differ from those who choose statistical victims. The original studies used random assignment; this deviation makes the replication a quasi-experiment at best and invalidates any comparison with the original causal claims.
matched_finding.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

ground_truth.modified_snippet: meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).
ground_truth.description: Reversed which condition has higher donations — IVE is now reversed (statistical > identifiable), contradicting the phenomenon being replicated and Table 11 descriptives

matched_finding.subcategory: direction of identifiable victim effect reversed
matched_finding.description: The core finding of the identifiable victim effect is that people donate more to an identifiable victim than to statistical victims. In the reported 'results' (based on simulated data), this effect is reversed: 'participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).' While this arises from random data, the manuscript presents this reversal as a finding and discusses it as a replication outcome without adequately flagging that the direction contradicts the foundational effect being replicated. Even if real, such a reversal would require substantial theoretical explanation.
matched_finding.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

matched_finding.subcategory: power analysis not included in main text
matched_finding.description: The manuscript states that power analysis is available only in supplementary materials, but provides no summary of minimum required sample size, assumed effect size, or achieved power in the main text. Power analysis is essential for evaluating whether the study was designed to detect the effects of interest. Without it in the main text, readers cannot assess whether observed null results reflect genuine absence of effects or inadequate power. This is especially important for a replication study where power to detect the original effect size is the key methodological question.
matched_finding.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary.

matched_finding.subcategory: availability heuristic incorrectly applied to explain identifiable victim effect
matched_finding.description: The introduction invokes the availability heuristic (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) to explain why an identifiable victim generates stronger affective responses than statistical victims. The availability heuristic is about ease of retrieving instances from memory to estimate frequency or probability—it is not the primary mechanism for the identifiable victim effect. The standard explanation involves the affect heuristic (Slovic et al., 2007), the singularity effect, or proportion dominance, all of which are explicitly discussed in Small et al. (2007). Misattributing the mechanism undermines the theoretical framing and misrepresents the literature.
matched_finding.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual.
